question: Write-ahead logging requires which order?
option_a: The changed data page reaches disk before any log record of that change
option_b: A checkpoint deletes the log before any data write
option_c: The log record of a change reaches stable storage before the changed data page does
option_d: Undo is never recorded, because recovery reads only the data pages
explanation: Write-ahead logging requires the log record describing a change to reach stable storage before the changed data page does. Otherwise a crash can leave a page that recovery cannot explain. Remember: the log is written before the data page.
hint: If the crash happens between the two writes, the log must already explain the change.
hint_2: Writing the data page first can leave a change that the log cannot undo or redo. A checkpoint does not delete the log before the write.
hint_3: The log goes first. That is the write-ahead rule.

question: A sparse index contains an entry for which of the following?
option_a: Every search-key value in the data file
option_c: Only some blocks or groups of records, not every search-key value
option_d: Every non-key column of every row
explanation: A sparse index has an entry for some blocks or groups of records, not for every search-key value. A dense index has an entry for every search-key value. Remember: sparse means some groups, and dense means every key.
hint: Dense means one index entry per search key. Sparse means fewer than that.
hint_2: An entry for every search key is a dense index. Nulls alone, and non-key columns, are not the definition.
hint_3: One entry can cover a block or a group, so the index is shorter than the data.

question: A decomposition is lossless when the natural join of the parts does which of the following?
option_a: Always adds spurious tuples that were not in the original relation
option_b: Drops the candidate key in every case and cannot be joined
option_d: Requires a Cartesian product with no join attribute and still loses tuples
explanation: A decomposition is lossless if the natural join of the decomposed relations restores exactly the original relation. Extra rows on that join mean the decomposition was lossy. Remember: lossless means the join gives the original rows back, with nothing added.
hint: Lossless means the split can be undone. Spurious tuples mean the opposite.
hint_2: Extra tuples are a lossy join. Dropping the key, or joining with no common attribute, is not the lossless test.
hint_3: The natural join brings back exactly the rows you started with.

question: Which command is a DCL command?
explanation: GRANT and REVOKE are data-control commands because they manage privileges. CREATE and DROP define objects, and UPDATE changes rows. Remember: GRANT is DCL.
hint: This family grants and revokes privileges. It is not data change and not table definition.
hint_2: CREATE and DROP are DDL. UPDATE is DML.
hint_3: GRANT is the data-control command.

question: A phantom read is which event?
option_a: A checkpoint that flushes dirty pages
option_b: A read of an uncommitted update that is later rolled back
option_c: Two writes of the same row with no intervening read
option_d: A second query in the same transaction sees a new row that another transaction inserted and committed
explanation: A phantom is a new committed row that appears in a repeated range query of the same transaction. A dirty read is a read of uncommitted data. Remember: a new row in a repeated range is a phantom.
hint: The same query, run twice, sees a different set of rows. The new row was committed.
hint_2: An uncommitted value that disappears is a dirty read. Two writes are not a phantom. A checkpoint is recovery work.
hint_3: A new row appears in a range that the transaction already queried.

question: A relation is in BCNF when which condition holds for every non-trivial functional dependency X determines A?
option_b: A is transitively dependent on X
option_c: X is a single non-key attribute
explanation: BCNF requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency, the determinant is a superkey. A dependency whose left side is not a superkey violates BCNF even when the right side is prime. Remember: in BCNF, every determinant is a superkey.
hint: BCNF looks at the left side of every non-trivial dependency, not only at non-prime attributes.
hint_2: A non-prime attribute on the right can be legal if the left side is a superkey. A non-key determinant is exactly what BCNF forbids. Transitive dependence is a violation, not the BCNF rule.
hint_3: Every determinant must be a superkey.

question: TCP slow start grows the congestion window, until a threshold or a loss, in which way?
option_a: It adds one segment per round trip and never increases faster than that
option_b: It is set by a DNS response
option_c: It stays fixed at one segment for the life of the connection
option_d: It roughly doubles each round trip, because each acknowledgement increases the window by one segment
explanation: In slow start, each acknowledgement increases the congestion window by one segment, so the window roughly doubles every round trip. After the threshold, congestion avoidance grows it more slowly. Remember: slow start doubles per round trip, despite the name.
hint: The name slow start is historical. The growth itself is exponential in the round-trip count.
hint_2: Adding one segment per round trip is congestion avoidance, after the threshold. The window does not stay at one, and DNS does not set it.
hint_3: One extra segment per acknowledgement doubles the window each round trip.

question: Count-to-infinity is a problem of which routing style?
option_a: Link-state flooding, where every router has a full map
explanation: In distance-vector routing, a router advertises distances and may accept a neighbour's route to a destination that actually goes through itself, so the metric climbs toward infinity after a failure. Link state avoids that by flooding the topology. Remember: count-to-infinity belongs to distance-vector routing.
hint: A router tells its neighbours a distance, and a failed route's distance climbs one hop at a time.
hint_2: Link state shares the map, so it does not count toward infinity in this way. Circuit switching and CSMA/CD are not routing-table exchanges.
hint_3: The distance-vector exchange is what produces count-to-infinity.

question: An IPv6 address is how long?
explanation: An IPv6 address is 128 bits, written as eight groups of hexadecimal. An IPv4 address is 32 bits. Remember: IPv6 is 128 bits.
hint: IPv4 is 32 bits. This version is four times that length.
hint_2: 32 bits is IPv4. 48 bits is a common MAC-address length. 256 is not the address length.
hint_3: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.

question: A CRC on a frame is used mainly to do which of the following?
option_a: Correct any burst error by itself in the usual link check
option_c: Choose a route between autonomous systems
explanation: A cyclic redundancy check detects errors by comparing a computed remainder with the received remainder. Correction, if any, is a separate mechanism such as retransmission. Remember: CRC detects, and a Hamming code is the usual correction example.
hint: The receiver recomputes a check and compares it with the received check.
hint_2: A usual CRC detects; it does not by itself tell the sender how to repair an arbitrary burst. Routing and MAC assignment are different jobs.
hint_3: The check is there to detect a damaged frame.

question: A host has address 172.16.5.70/26. What is its network address?
explanation: A /26 splits the last octet into blocks of 64. The block containing 70 starts at 64, so the network address is 172.16.5.64, and the broadcast address is 172.16.5.127. Remember: for a /26, clear the last 6 bits of the host address.
hint: A /26 has a block size of 64 in the last octet. Find which block contains 70.
hint_2: 0 is the previous block. 128 is the next block. 70 is a host address inside the block, not the network address.
hint_3: 70 falls in the block that starts at 64.

question: If the Round Robin time quantum is made extremely small, which effect dominates?
option_a: The scheduler behaves like First Come First Served
option_b: Context-switch overhead becomes a large fraction of CPU time
option_d: Belady's anomaly disappears from the pager
explanation: A tiny quantum causes a context switch after almost every brief run, so switch overhead dominates. A very large quantum makes Round Robin behave like First Come First Served. Remember: too small a quantum wastes the CPU on switching.
hint: A very large quantum pushes Round Robin toward one familiar non-preemptive scheduler. A very small quantum does the opposite harm.
hint_2: First Come First Served behaviour appears when the quantum is huge, not tiny. Quantum size does not remove deadlock or Belady's anomaly.
hint_3: The CPU spends its time switching instead of running the jobs.

question: A zombie process is which of the following?
option_a: A process that has finished, but whose parent has not yet collected its exit status
option_b: A process running on two CPUs at the same moment by definition
option_c: A thread that holds no locks
option_d: A dirty page in the page cache
explanation: A zombie has exited, but its parent has not collected the exit status, so the process-table entry remains. It is not a running process and not a dirty page. Remember: exited and not yet reaped means a zombie.
hint: The process has exited. A small record remains until the parent calls wait.
hint_2: Two CPUs, an unlocked thread, and a dirty page are not the definition of a zombie.
hint_3: Finished, but not yet waited for, means a zombie.

question: In deadlock avoidance, a state is safe when which of the following is true?
option_a: There is an order of process completions that can satisfy every remaining need from currently available resources, releasing each process's allocation as it finishes
option_b: Every process already holds at least one resource, which is required for safety
option_d: No process has declared a maximum claim
explanation: A state is safe when there is an order in which each process can obtain its remaining need, finish, and release its allocation for the others. The Banker's algorithm refuses a request that would leave no such order. Remember: safe means there is a way for every process to finish.
hint: The Banker's algorithm looks for an order in which every process can finish.
hint_2: Holding a resource is not what makes a state safe. A deadlock is an unsafe, already-stuck state. The algorithm needs the maximum claims.
hint_3: A safe state has a completion sequence that never gets stuck.

question: Compaction is a remedy for which problem?
option_a: External fragmentation in variable-size memory allocation
option_b: A dirty read in a database
explanation: Compaction moves allocated variable-size blocks so that scattered free holes become one usable region. It addresses external fragmentation, not a concurrency anomaly. Remember: holes between blocks, slid together, means compaction.
hint: Free memory exists, but it is broken into holes too small for the next request.
hint_2: A dirty read, a lost segment, and a weak hash are not fixed by sliding allocated blocks together.
hint_3: Slide the allocated blocks together so the free space becomes one hole.

question: A multilevel feedback queue changes a process's priority mainly according to which behaviour?
option_a: The length of the process name
option_b: How the process has used the CPU so far, so a CPU-bound process sinks and an interactive process can stay higher
option_d: The number of open SQL cursors only
explanation: A multilevel feedback queue lowers a process that uses its whole quantum and can favour a process that blocks quickly, which is typical of interactive work. The priority is feedback from observed behaviour, not a fixed label. Remember: CPU-bound work sinks, and interactive work can stay higher.
hint: The process is not stuck in the queue it started in. Its recent CPU use moves it.
hint_2: The name, the terminal colour, and the cursor count are not the feedback signal.
hint_3: A process that burns its quantum sinks. A process that blocks for I/O can stay favoured.

question: The load factor of a hash table is which ratio?
option_a: The number of stored keys divided by the number of slots
option_b: The number of slots divided by the key size in bits
option_c: The chain length multiplied by the table's base address
option_d: The height of an AVL tree used as a secondary index in every hash table
explanation: The load factor is the number of stored keys divided by the number of slots. A high load factor lengthens chains or probe sequences, so the table is resized. Remember: load factor equals keys divided by slots.
hint: It measures how full the table is.
hint_2: Key size, a base address, and an AVL height are not the load factor.
hint_3: Keys divided by slots is the load factor.

question: In a binary search tree, deleting a node that has two children is usually done by replacing it with which node?
option_a: Either child, with no further change to the tree
option_b: Its in-order successor or its in-order predecessor
option_c: The root of the whole tree, in every deletion
option_d: A newly inserted null node that becomes the parent of both children
explanation: A node with two children is replaced by its in-order successor or predecessor, which has at most one child, and that node is then removed from its old place. Either child cannot be copied in without breaking the search order. Remember: two children means replace with the in-order neighbour.
hint: The replacement must keep every left descendant smaller and every right descendant larger.
hint_2: Either child can break the search order. The root is not the general replacement. A new null cannot take the node's place as a value.
hint_3: The next key in sorted order, or the previous one, can take the node's place.

question: In the usual case, C passes an argument by which method?
option_a: By value, so the function receives a copy
option_b: By reference for every int, with no copy and no way to pass an address explicitly
option_c: By name, as in Algol, for every bank program written in C
explanation: C passes arguments by value, so the function receives a copy and assigning to the parameter does not change the caller's variable. The caller can pass a pointer if the function must update the original object. Remember: C is pass by value, and a pointer is how the callee reaches the original.
hint: The callee can change its parameter without changing the caller's variable, unless an address was passed.
hint_2: C does not pass every int by reference. Pass by name is not the C rule. A trigger is not a calling convention.
hint_3: The function gets a copy. To let it change the caller's object, the caller passes a pointer.

question: Which Java feature lets one class satisfy several contracts without extending several classes?
option_a: Extending multiple classes, which Java allows in the same way as C++
option_c: A macro that copies method bodies
option_d: A friend declaration, which is the Java keyword for this feature
explanation: A Java class extends one class and may implement any number of interfaces, so several contracts do not require multiple class inheritance. C++ multiple inheritance is not the Java rule. Remember: many interfaces, one parent class.
hint: Java allows one parent class. The way to take on several type contracts is different.
hint_2: Java does not allow a class to extend multiple classes. Macros and friend are not the Java mechanism.
hint_3: A class may implement more than one interface.
